usage: The default verb is 하다; 청소 is the object, so use 를.
Put the place right before 청소 with no particle: 방 청소, 화장실 청소.
대(大) 'big' + 청소 = a thorough top-to-bottom clean.
청소기 (cleaner machine) is 'vacuum'; you 돌리다 (spin/run) it, not 하다.
examples: 저는 청소를 해요.
I do the cleaning.
Simple frame: 청소 + 를 + 해요 is the core pattern to memorize.
주말마다 방을 청소해요.
I clean my room every weekend.
Everyday: 청소하다 can take a direct object (방을) without saying 청소를.
청소가 다 끝나서 집이 반짝반짝해요.
Cleaning is all done, so the house is sparkling.
Real life: here 청소 is the subject with 가, and 끝나다 means it 'finished'.
nuance: 청소 is Sino-Korean, 清掃 (清 'clear' + 掃 'sweep'), so its core sense is sweeping a space clean — floors, rooms, a car, a screen. Its everyday verb is 하다 (청소하다 / 청소를 하다). Do not confuse it with 정리 (整理), which is tidying/arranging objects into order: you 청소 the dust and grime off a surface, but you 정리 the scattered books on a desk; a messy-but-clean desk needs 정리, a dusty floor needs 청소. Register is neutral — kids and adults all say 청소해요. The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'I clean' tempts learners to make 청소 the subject (청소가 해요 ✗), but 청소 is the thing being done, so it must be the OBJECT — 청소를 해요 (○). Also note 청소기 is the vacuum, and you 돌리다 it, never 청소를 하다 the machine itself.

mistakes: 청소가 해요. ✗ → 청소를 해요. ○
'Cleaning' is the action you perform, not the actor. With 하다 it is the object, so it takes 를, never 가.
Use 청소를 해요 or just 청소해요.
방을 정리해요 vs 방을 청소해요
Saying 청소 when you only put toys away is wrong — that is tidying. 청소 is for removing dirt/dust, 정리 is for arranging things.
Put-things-in-order = 정리; scrub/sweep dust = 청소.

usage: The washing action; 빨래 is the object so it takes 를.
After washing you 널다 (spread out to dry) the wet clothes.
Dry clothes are 개다 (folded); note 개다, not 접다, for laundry.
Here 빨래 is the subject with 가; 마르다 = to dry out.
examples: 오늘 빨래를 해요.
I do the laundry today.
Simple frame: 빨래 + 를 + 해요, the basic chore pattern.
빨래가 많아서 세탁기를 두 번 돌렸어요.
There was a lot of laundry, so I ran the washer twice.
Everyday: 빨래 as subject (가) + 많다; the machine 세탁기 you 돌리다.
빨래를 다 널고 나서 커피 한잔하고 싶어요.
After hanging all the laundry, I want a coffee.
Real life: 널다 = hang to dry, and 고 나서 = 'after doing'.
nuance: 빨래 is a native Korean word (not Sino-Korean) and is genuinely double-sided: it means both the ACTIVITY of washing clothes (빨래를 하다) and the physical LAUNDRY ITEMS themselves (빨래가 많다 'there's a lot of wash'). Its root is the verb 빨다 'to wash by hand/rub'. The near-synonym is 세탁 (洗濯), the stiffer Sino-Korean word you see on signs and machines — 세탁기 (washer), 세탁소 (dry-cleaner's), 세탁 코스; in casual home talk Koreans say 빨래, in formal/written contexts 세탁. The big pitfall for English speakers is treating 'do the laundry' as making something: 빨래를 만들다 (✗) is nonsense — laundry is washed, so it is 빨래를 하다. Second, the drying chore is 널다 (널어요), not 걸다; and folding finished laundry is 개다, not 접다. Choose the verb to the stage: 하다 → 널다 → 개다.

mistakes: 빨래를 만들어요. ✗ → 빨래를 해요. ○
'Make laundry' copies English literally; clothes are washed, not manufactured. The verb for the chore is 하다.
Use 빨래를 해요 or 빨래해요.
빨래를 걸어요. ✗ → 빨래를 널어요. ○
걸다 is hanging one item on a hook; spreading wet wash out to dry is its own verb, 널다.
Wet laundry to dry = 널다; fold dry laundry = 개다.

usage: The chore takes 하다; 설거지 is the object with 를.
설거지 as subject with 가; 쌓이다 = to accumulate.
거리 = 'stuff/material for'; 설거지거리 = the dirty-dish workload.
당번 = person on rotation duty; common in homes and dorms.
examples: 제가 설거지를 해요.
I wash the dishes.
Simple frame: 설거지 + 를 + 해요, the whole-meal cleanup.
밥 먹고 나서 바로 설거지해요.
Right after eating, I do the dishes.
Everyday: 고 나서 'after'; 설거지하다 written solid is most natural here.
설거지가 너무 많이 쌓여서 한숨이 나왔어요.
So many dishes piled up that I sighed.
Real life: 설거지 as subject + 쌓이다; 한숨이 나오다 = a sigh comes out.
nuance: 설거지 is a native Korean word for the specific chore of washing the dishes, pots, and utensils AFTER a meal — it bundles the whole task, not one plate. It always pairs with 하다 (설거지하다). The crucial contrast is with the verb 씻다 'to wash/rinse': you 씻다 an individual object or body part (사과를 씻다 'wash an apple', 손을 씻다 'wash hands'), but the household routine of clearing the table's dishes is the noun 설거지(를 하다). So '설거지를 씻다' (✗) sounds like washing the act itself. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that overlap — English uses 'wash the dishes', tempting 접시를 씻다, which is acceptable for literally rinsing plates, but the everyday CHORE Koreans name is 설거지하다. Note also it is one fixed word: don't break it into pieces. Common partners: 설거지가 쌓이다 (pile up), 설거지 당번 (dish duty).

씻다 takes a concrete thing (hands, fruit, a plate). 설거지 is the named chore, so its verb is 하다.
Chore = 설거지를 해요; rinse one item = 접시를 씻다.
설거지를 만들어요. ✗ → 설거지를 해요. ○
Like other chores, you don't 'make' dish-washing. 하다 is the verb that activates the chore noun.
Always 설거지하다 for the action.

usage: The action takes 하다; 요리 is the object with 를.
요리 as the finished dish; nationality goes in front with no particle.
요리법 (法 'method') is the native-style word; 레시피 is the loanword.
잘하다 'do well' fused; 요리를 잘해요 = a good cook.
examples: 저는 요리를 해요.
I cook.
Simple frame: 요리 + 를 + 해요, the basic 'I cook' sentence.
주말에 한국 요리를 만들어 보고 싶어요.
On weekends I want to try making Korean dishes.
Everyday: here 요리 = the dish, so 만들다 'make' is fine; 아 보다 = 'try doing'.
엄마 요리가 세상에서 제일 맛있어요.
Mom's cooking is the most delicious in the world.
Real life: 요리 as the result-food; 제일 = the most.
nuance: 요리 is Sino-Korean, 料理 (料 'ingredients/measure' + 理 'manage/arrange'), literally 'managing ingredients', and it covers BOTH the act of cooking (요리를 하다) and the finished DISH/cuisine (한국 요리 'Korean cuisine', 엄마 요리 'mom's cooking'). Watch the verb split by meaning: for the ACTIVITY use 하다 (요리해요), but for producing a specific dish use 만들다 'make' (김치찌개를 만들어요). The near-synonym 음식 (飮食) means 'food' as a substance you eat or buy, while 요리 implies it was prepared/cooked with some skill — a bag of chips is 음식, not 요리. The English-speaker pitfall is saying 요리를 먹다 to mean 'I cook and eat': 요리를 먹다 actually means 'eat a dish', so for the act you need 요리를 하다. Also 요리사 (師 'master') is a professional chef. Common partners: 요리를 잘하다, 집밥 요리 (home-cooked food).

mistakes: 요리를 먹어요 (meaning 'I cook'). ✗ → 요리를 해요. ○
요리 is two-sided; 먹다 only fits the dish-meaning ('eat a dish'). For the act of cooking the verb is 하다.
Cook the action = 요리를 해요; eat the dish = 요리를 먹다.
이 요리는 음식이에요 misuse
음식 = food generally; 요리 = a prepared dish. Calling instant snacks 요리 overstates the effort.
Prepared/cooked = 요리; food in general = 음식.

usage: The core verb is 버리다 (discard), with 쓰레기 as object 를.
통 = bin/container; 쓰레기통 is the can you throw trash into.
Korea sorts food waste separately; 음식물 (foodstuff) + 쓰레기.
분리수거 = sorted collection, the legally required recycling sort.
examples: 쓰레기를 버려요.
I throw out the trash.
Simple frame: 쓰레기 + 를 + 버리다, the key verb that is NOT 하다.
오늘은 음식물 쓰레기 버리는 날이에요.
Today is the day to take out food waste.
Everyday: 버리는 날 = 'the day for throwing out'; food waste is its own category.
쓰레기를 아무 데나 버리면 안 돼요.
You mustn't throw trash just anywhere.
Real life: 면 안 되다 = 'must not'; 아무 데나 = 'just any place'.
nuance: 쓰레기 is a native Korean noun meaning garbage/waste, and unlike the chore nouns around it, its verb is NOT 하다 but 버리다 'to throw away/discard' (쓰레기를 버리다). The near-synonym 쓰레기 vs 폐기물 (廢棄物, formal 'waste matter') splits by register: 쓰레기 is the everyday spoken word, 폐기물 is industrial/legal (산업 폐기물 'industrial waste'). Used figuratively, 쓰레기 is also a harsh insult for a contemptible person ('that guy is 쓰레기' = scum), so be careful aiming it at people. The big English-speaker pitfall is overusing 하다: 쓰레기를 해요 (✗) is meaningless — trash is acted on with 버리다, or sorted with 분리수거하다. Second pitfall: 'take out the trash' should not become 쓰레기를 가지고 나가다 mechanically; the idiomatic phrase is just 쓰레기를 버리다 or 쓰레기를 내놓다 (put it out). Korea strictly sorts 음식물 쓰레기 (food waste) and recycling, so 분리수거 is an essential collocation.

mistakes: 쓰레기를 해요. ✗ → 쓰레기를 버려요. ○
쓰레기 is not a 하다-chore; you discard it. The verb is 버리다.
Throw out = 쓰레기를 버리다; sort = 분리수거하다.
사람한테 함부로 쓰레기라고 하기
Literally 'trash', but as slang it means 'scumbag', a strong insult, so don't apply it to people lightly.
For objects only unless you truly mean the insult.

usage: The action takes 하다; 정리 is the object with 를.
정리하다 can take a direct object (방을) — arrange that space.
Fixed 4-syllable pair 整理整頓; emphasizes everything in its place.
정리 also works on abstractions — sorting ideas, plans, feelings.
examples: 책상을 정리해요.
I tidy the desk.
Simple frame: object + 정리하다 = put that thing in order.
이사 가기 전에 짐을 정리하고 있어요.
I'm sorting my stuff before moving.
Everyday: 고 있다 = ongoing; 짐 = belongings/luggage to arrange.
회의 내용을 정리해서 메일로 보낼게요.
I'll summarize the meeting and email it.
Real life: here 정리 = 'summarize/compile' information, a common office sense.
nuance: 정리 is Sino-Korean, 整理 (整 'arrange/orderly' + 理 'manage'), meaning to put scattered things into order — and its scope is broad: physical stuff (책상을 정리하다 'tidy a desk'), abstract ideas (생각을 정리하다 'organize thoughts'), even finishing/winding up (관계를 정리하다 'end a relationship', 일을 정리하다 'wrap up affairs'). The verb is 하다. The sharp contrast is with 청소 (清掃): 정리 = arranging objects into their places; 청소 = removing dirt/dust by sweeping or wiping. A dusty but neat room needs 청소; a clean-floored but cluttered room needs 정리; Koreans often pair them — 청소하고 정리하다. The English-speaker pitfall is 정리를 만들다 (✗), copying 'make tidy'; the chore noun is activated by 하다 only. Also don't assume 정리 = mere cleaning — its summarize/conclude senses surprise learners, so 'I'll 정리 my notes' means compile/summarize them, not scrub them.

mistakes: 정리를 만들어요. ✗ → 정리를 해요. ○
'Make' doesn't apply; the chore/action noun pairs with 하다.
Always 정리하다 for the action.
방이 더러울 때 정리하다 vs 청소하다
If the floor is dirty, 정리 (arranging) doesn't help — you need 청소 (cleaning). Mixing them mislabels the task.
Arrange clutter = 정리; remove dirt = 청소.

usage: The action takes 하다; 샤워 is the object with 를.
기 (器 'device') turns the loanword into the fixture: the showerhead/handset.
a cold shower / shower with cold water
Temperature goes in front, or the water as means with 로/으로.
고 나오다 = 'after doing, come out'; the natural post-shower phrase.
examples: 저는 샤워를 해요.
I take a shower.
Simple frame: 샤워 + 를 + 해요, even though 'shower' is a loanword it still needs 하다.
아침마다 따뜻한 물로 샤워해요.
Every morning I shower with warm water.
Everyday: 로 marks the water as the means; 마다 = 'every'.
운동하고 땀이 나서 얼른 샤워하러 갔어요.
I sweated from exercise, so I quickly went to shower.
Real life: 으러 가다 = 'go in order to'; 땀이 나다 = to sweat.
nuance: 샤워 is a loanword from English 'shower', and like other action loanwords it Koreanizes by attaching 하다 (샤워하다 / 샤워를 하다) — it specifically means standing under running water. Contrast it with 목욕 (沐浴), which is soaking/bathing in a tub or at a bathhouse (목욕탕): a quick rinse standing up is 샤워, a long soak is 목욕. Both differ from 세수 (洗手), which is washing only the face. Register is fully neutral. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is dropping 하다 because 'shower' already feels like a verb in English — but 샤워 alone is just the noun; you must say 샤워하다, never use 샤워 bare as a verb. Second pitfall: choosing the wrong washing word — for the whole body standing up it's 샤워, not 씻다 broadly (though 씻다 'wash up' is a loose casual cover term) and not 세수 (face only). The water you use takes 로/으로: 찬물로 샤워하다.

샤워를 먹어요. ✗ → 샤워를 해요. ○

usage: The action takes 하다; 세수 is the object with 를.
고 = 'and then'; the natural morning sequence after washing the face.
Idiom for a too-hasty, barely-there face wash, like a cat's lick.
to wash the face with cold water
The water takes 로; common to wake oneself up.
examples: 저는 세수를 해요.
I wash my face.
Simple frame: 세수 + 를 + 해요; remember it's the FACE only.
아침에 일어나서 세수부터 해요.
After waking, I wash my face first.
Everyday: 부터 = 'starting with/first'; the first thing in the routine.
어제는 피곤해서 세수도 안 하고 잤어요.
Yesterday I was so tired I slept without even washing my face.
Real life: 도 안 하고 = 'without even doing'; 피곤하다 = tired.
nuance: 세수 is Sino-Korean, 洗手 (洗 'wash' + 手 'hand'), and although it literally says 'wash hands', in modern usage it means washing the FACE (and hands) — the morning/evening face-wash, not the body. Its verb is 하다 (세수하다). Be careful with the three washing words: 세수 = face; 샤워 = whole-body standing rinse; 목욕 = soaking bath; and the plain verb 씻다 'wash' is the broad casual umbrella ('얼굴을 씻다' literally 'wash the face' is also said). Register is neutral and very everyday. The English-speaker pitfall comes straight from the hanja: learners read 洗手 and assume it means 'wash hands' for hygiene — but to say 'wash your hands' (before eating, after the toilet) Koreans use 손을 씻다, not 세수. Using 세수 for the whole body is also wrong (that's 샤워/목욕). A nice idiom to know: 고양이 세수, a 'cat wash', for splashing your face so quickly you barely cleaned it.

mistakes: 밥 먹기 전에 세수하세요 (meaning 'wash hands'). ✗ → 손을 씻으세요. ○
Despite the 手 'hand' hanja, 세수 = washing the face. Hand-washing for hygiene is 손을 씻다.
Hands = 손을 씻다; face routine = 세수하다.
세수로 몸을 씻어요. ✗ → 샤워해요 / 목욕해요. ○
세수 covers only the face, never the body. Whole-body washing is 샤워 (rinse) or 목욕 (soak).
Body = 샤워/목욕; face = 세수.

usage: Both work; 양치질 is the fuller noun, both take 하다 with 를.
The default dental routine collocation; 고 = 'and then'.
양치 modifies the cup and tools used for brushing/rinsing.
가글(gargle) is the extra rinse step after 양치.
examples: 저는 양치를 해요.
I brush my teeth.
Simple frame: 양치 + 를 + 해요; or just 양치해요.
밥을 먹고 나서 꼭 양치해요.
I always brush right after meals.
Everyday: 고 나서 'after'; 꼭 = 'without fail'.
자기 전에 양치하는 거 잊지 마세요.
Don't forget to brush before bed.
Real life: 는 거 nominalizes the action; 잊지 마세요 = 'don't forget'.
nuance: 양치 (often the fuller 양치질) means brushing the teeth; it derives from hanja 養齒 (養 'nurture/care for' + 齒 'tooth') — 'caring for the teeth' — with the native suffix 질 (a 'doing of') giving 양치질. Its verb is 하다 (양치하다 / 양치질하다). The near-synonym 이를 닦다 'to scrub the teeth' (이 'tooth' + 닦다 'wipe/polish') is fully interchangeable in daily speech — 양치하다 = 이를 닦다 — though 닦다 highlights the scrubbing motion while 양치 names the routine including rinsing. Register is neutral; parents say it to kids constantly. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 솔질 or inventing 'teeth-brushing' literally; just use 양치하다 or 이를 닦다. Another trap is forgetting it's a noun: 양치 standing alone isn't a verb, so you must add 하다. And don't say 양치를 먹다 (✗) — 먹다 'eat' has no place in a brushing phrase. The toothbrush itself is 칫솔, the toothpaste 치약.

mistakes: 양치를 먹어요. ✗ → 양치를 해요. ○
먹다 doesn't belong to brushing; the chore noun is activated by 하다.
Use 양치해요 or 이를 닦아요.
이빨을 닦다 in polite speech
이빨 is a coarse/animal word for teeth; in normal/polite speech use 이 or 치아. So 이를 닦다, not 이빨을 닦다.
Polite: 양치하다 / 이를 닦다; avoid 이빨.

usage: The activity takes 하다; 산책 is the object with 를.
to go out for a walk
나가다 = go out; stresses leaving the house to stroll.
산책 as the noun event; 강아지 산책(을) 시키다 = walk the dog.
Place of the stroll takes 에서 (action location).
examples: 저는 산책을 해요.
I take a walk.
Simple frame: 산책 + 를 + 해요, a leisurely stroll.
저녁 먹고 동네 한 바퀴 산책해요.
After dinner I stroll one loop around the neighborhood.
Everyday: 한 바퀴 = 'one lap'; 동네 = neighborhood.
날씨가 좋아서 강아지랑 천천히 산책하고 왔어요.
The weather was nice, so I went for a slow walk with my dog.
Real life: 랑 = 'with' (casual); 고 오다 = 'go do and come back'.
nuance: 산책 is Sino-Korean, 散策 (散 'scatter/disperse' + 策 'walking stick'), poetically 'wandering with a stick' — i.e. a relaxed, purpose-free stroll for pleasure or fresh air. Its verb is 하다 (산책하다 / 산책을 하다). The key contrast is with the plain verb 걷다 'to walk': 걷다 is the physical act of walking (to a destination, for transport, for exercise pace), while 산책 is the leisurely OUTING itself — you 산책하다 in a park to relax, but you 걷다 to the station because the bus didn't come. Also 산책 ≠ 등산 (登山 'climb a mountain', hiking). Register is neutral and pleasant. The English-speaker pitfall is 산책을 가다 (✗) modeled on 'go for a walk' — the chore/activity noun normally takes 하다, so use 산책하다; if you want the 'go out' nuance, say 산책(을) 나가다 or 산책하러 가다 'go in order to stroll'. Don't confuse it with simply 걷다 when the point is leisure.

'Go for a walk' translated piece-by-piece is unnatural; the activity noun pairs with 하다, or use 하러 가다 for 'go to'.
Stroll = 산책하다; go to stroll = 산책하러 가다.
역까지 산책했어요 (meaning 'walked to the station'). ✗ → 역까지 걸어갔어요. ○
산책 is leisure, not getting somewhere. Walking to a destination is 걷다/걸어가다.
Leisure stroll = 산책; walk to a place = 걸어가다.

usage: The idiomatic verb is 취하다 (take/assume), more than 하다: 휴식을 취하다.
휴식 modifies 시간; the scheduled break (class, work).
잠깐 = briefly; announced before a pause in meetings or workouts.
휴식 as subject with 이; pairs with 필요하다 'be needed'.
examples: 휴식이 필요해요.
I need rest.
Simple frame: 휴식 + 이 + 필요해요; here it's the subject.
회의 중간에 십 분 동안 휴식 시간을 가졌어요.
We took a ten-minute break in the middle of the meeting.
Everyday: 휴식 시간을 가지다 = 'have a break'; 동안 = 'for (duration)'.
요즘 너무 무리해서 푹 휴식을 취하고 싶어요.
I've overdone it lately, so I want to rest fully.
Real life: 휴식을 취하다 (formal 'take rest'); 푹 = thoroughly/deeply.
nuance: 휴식 is Sino-Korean, 休息 (休 'rest' + 息 'breathe/pause'), 'resting and catching one's breath', a somewhat formal/written noun for taking a break. Its most idiomatic verb is 휴식을 취하다 'to take rest' (취하다 = take/assume), and 휴식하다 also exists, but in casual conversation Koreans far more often use the plain native verb 쉬다 'to rest' — '집에서 쉬어요' sounds natural where '집에서 휴식해요' sounds stiff. So the contrast is register: 휴식 = formal/signage/health-advice tone (충분한 휴식, 휴식 시간), 쉬다 = everyday speech. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 휴식 like a casual verb and overusing 휴식하다 in chat — prefer 쉬다 there. Also, because it's a noun, you cannot leave it bare for the action: pair it with 취하다/하다, or switch to 쉬다. Common collocations: 휴식 시간, 휴식을 취하다, 충분한 휴식, 잠깐 휴식.

휴식하다 is stiff for casual talk; with friends the natural verb is 쉬다.

usage: The action takes 하다; 외출 is the object with 를.
준비 = preparation; 외출 준비(를) 하다 = prep before leaving.
중 (中 'in the middle of') marks the away status: 외출 중이에요.
to not feel like going out
기 싫다 = 'hate to do'; common homebody phrase.
examples: 저는 외출을 해요.
I go out.
Simple frame: 외출 + 를 + 해요; leaving the house.
비가 와서 오늘은 외출 안 했어요.
It rained, so I didn't go out today.
Everyday: 안 + 했어요 negates; 와서 = 'because it came (rained)'.
외출하기 전에 가스 불을 껐는지 꼭 확인하세요.
Before going out, be sure to check you turned off the gas.
Real life: 기 전에 = 'before doing'; 는지 확인하다 = 'check whether'.
nuance: 외출 is Sino-Korean, 外出 (外 'outside' + 出 'go out/exit'), 'going out of the house', and its verb is 하다 (외출하다 / 외출을 하다). It specifically means leaving home to go outside, often briefly. The near-synonym contrast: 외출 is leaving the HOUSE for a short while (외출 중 'stepped out'); 나가다 is the plain verb 'go out/exit' (any space); and 외박 (外泊) is the contrasting word for staying out OVERNIGHT (sleeping away from home) — useful so learners don't mix 외출 (out and back) with 외박 (out overnight). 외출 carries a slightly neutral-formal tone, common in notes ('외출 중입니다' 'I'm out'). The English-speaker pitfall is 외출을 가다 (✗), built from 'go out' — the activity noun takes 하다, so 외출하다; if you want a destination, name it with 가다 (시내에 가다 'go downtown') instead of forcing 외출 with 가다. Also remember it's a noun: don't use 외출 bare for the action. Collocations: 외출 준비, 외출 중, 외출 금지 (grounded/no-going-out).
